extracted.intended_audience: interactive fiction authors, entrants, judges, and players (including newcomers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards for interactive fiction (IF) entries to the Interactive Fiction Competition, covering core expectations about text-centered gameplay and the three main IF forms (parser IF, choice-based/CYOA, and hypertext), plus accessibility and resource recommendations for new players.

rubrics_metrics.name: IFComp entries are videogames whose player interactions center on text
rubrics_metrics.description: IFComp entries are videogames whose player interactions center on text. They communicate to their players primarily by displaying text, and players respond in turn by pushing text back at them, one way or another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The site emphasizes that the core defining facet for entries is text-centered interaction rather than specific engine or UI. This is the broad, stable criterion the competition uses while allowing stylistic evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parser IF: natural-language parser accepting typed instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Parser IF features a natural-language parser that accepts typed-in instructions from the player for what the main character ought to do next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-made (and thoroughly tested) parser game will accept many reasonable inputs and respond appropriately (examples: GO NORTH, LOOK AT THE CAT, ASK THE CAT ABOUT THE DOOR). Common anti-pattern: responding frequently with "That's not a verb I recognize" or similarly unhelpful messages. Parser IF demands acquired skill and benefits from clear cues and tutorials for new players.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parser IF: encourage open, player-directed exploration
rubrics_metrics.description: Parser games done well can excel at creating a sense of open, player-directed exploration—whether through physical geographies, abstract conceptual spaces, or complex conversations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design should allow players to explore broadly and interact with the world in many reasonable ways. Testing for many reasonable inputs and providing meaningful responses supports this exploratory quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parser IF: provide tutorials, player-aids, or beginner-friendly design
rubrics_metrics.description: Because parser interfaces have a learning curve, strong parser IF often provides tools, guides, and other player-aids (including in-game tutorial voices or optional prologues) to help new players learn conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given include The Dreamhold and Bronze (tutorial voices), The Dreamhold/Blue Lacuna/Counterfeit Monkey (prologues or optional tutorial sections). Good practice: include optional tutorials, pocket references, or beginner-friendly openings so new players can get comfortable before the game opens up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice-based IF (CYOA): explicit choices that drive momentum through story
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice-based IF gives the player, after certain passages of story text, a list of possible actions; the player picks one and the story continues, taking that choice into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice-based games emphasize maintaining narrative momentum rather than free spatial exploration. Well-crafted CYOA entries make each choice move the tale forward and create a satisfying feeling of investment in the story's outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypertext IF: clickable text links and site-like navigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypertext IF invites players to click on highlighted words or phrases in the text to move between scenes, expand text in-place, or trigger other effects—similar to navigating a website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-crafted hypertext game trades parser ambiguity for a network of clearly marked passageways; good hypertext design can provide a distinctive exploratory experience. Modern hypertext IF is often implemented in Twine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different IF forms afford different player experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Parser IF, CYOA, and hypertext each provide distinct interaction models and player experiences—open exploration (parser), momentum-driven choice (CYOA), and link-based labyrinthine navigation (hypertext).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should choose the form that best fits their design goals and be mindful of the affordances and limits of each (e.g., parser supports wide interaction vocabularies, CYOA supports readable branching narrative, hypertext supports clickable, spatially-organized passages).

rubrics_metrics.name: IFComp’s inclusive, non-prescriptive stance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Interactive Fiction Competition avoids taking a prescriptive stance as to what is and isn’t IF, allowing itself to act as an expression of the community’s evolving definition of the term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the competition recognizes historical tendencies (many past entries have been parser-based), it accommodates experimental works and newer tools (e.g., Twine, ChoiceScript). Authors are not strictly confined to one definition of IF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommend community resources and exemplar works for learning and evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: New players and authors are pointed to community resources (Interactive Fiction Database, community forum, handpicked newcomer-friendly games, past IFComp winners and top entries) as guidance and exemplars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using these resources helps authors and players understand conventions, discover tutorial-style games, and see high-quality examples. The page lists specific recommended works and resources for both learning to play parser IF and for sampling notable IF.
